newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq, U.N. complete food distribution plans.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, U.N. complete food distribution plans.

text.p: Iraq and the United Nations have completed their food distribution plans to cover the next six months of oil exports and would soon send them to the U.N. for approval, Iraq's U.N. coordintor said on Thursday.

Staffan de Mistura said U.N. agencies had their plan for the three northern provinces of Dahouk, Arbil and Sulaimaniya, currently outside the control of the central government in Baghdad, ready since June 29.

He said Iraqi authorities told him their plan for the centre and south of Iraq "was also ready but it needed some fine tuning" to incorporate both into a unified national programme before presenting them to the United Nations.
Iraq is permitted to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months, under U.N. supervision, to alleviate hardship caused by U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Baghdad for invading Kuwait in 1991.

The oil plan was first started in December last year and the U.N. Security Council renewed it for another 180 days on June 8. But the exports have been held up pending the completion of the procurement and distribution plans by the government.

In the first six months Iraq earned about $1.3 billion, of which $260 million was earmarked for the northern provinces. De Mistura said Iraq would earn a similar amount of money in the next six months.
Iraq needs U.N. approval of both plans to be able to start pumping partial oil sales to world markets again.
"We are in the process of finalising the distribution plan which according to the government is crucial in order to decide on the renewal of oil sales," de Mistura told Reuters.
"We have done our part and the ball is now in the court of the government," he added.

De Mistura said about one million tonnes of food from the first partial sales had arrived in Iraq. He said Iraq needed to resume sales again to keep humanitarian commodities arriving on a steady basis.
He said Iraq's current distribution plan was based on the experience earned in the past few months. "There will be emphasis on vulnerable groups, the handicapped and malnourished children," he said.
He said deliveries of medical items were slow "and we feel sad about it but they are moving."
Iraq has repeatedly complained about the sluggish pace of approving contracts under the deal by the U.N. sanctions committee but de Mistura said he did not expect further delays.
"We are very confident there will be a massive arrival of food and medicine and the Iraqis will be able to have full rations under the oil deal," de Mistura said.
